S4yX3N48IvY.title: My Maxims, Part 3
S4yX3N48IvY.one_line: After praising the encampments and lamenting the ummah's low ambitions, two maxims: Islam is transmitted through qualified teachers, and you must work with people you disagree with.
S4yX3N48IvY.summary: He begins with the shift in public opinion and the campus encampments against university investment in the genocide in Gaza, hoping that courage spreads to the Muslim world. Muslims everywhere share the same hopes and fears yet their voice is ignored, and they have accepted it, setting the bar at a functioning masjid and enough money. That is why he keeps talking about this: earlier imams could discuss abstract topics because Muslims were respected. Change will come from within, as the Prophet was told the ummah would only be undone by itself, and must begin with decisions only Allah sees. His first maxim is that Islam is an oral tradition passed through permission from teachers: one should not preach from books or online videos, and a community needs qualified scholars before buildings, just as doctors learn on rotations. He describes his fear of being accountable for speaking in the Prophet's place. His second maxim is that you do not have to agree with everyone to work with them. Citing the hadith that the believer who mixes with people and bears their harm is better, and Abu Bakr's correction of how people misread 5:105, he insists there is no clean exit from the community, even for those who have been burnt; we sail or sink together.

outline.heading: Opening
The winds changing: campus encampments
outline.gist: Public opinion is shifting and a new generation sees what was unclear before: students worldwide hold encampments against their universities investing in a state carrying out a systematic genocide that the world condemns in pathetic, plainly biased wording.

outline.heading: May the courage be contagious
outline.gist: He appreciates the students' courage and hopes it spreads to every field and to Muslims in majority and minority countries, so they unite their voices for the 35,000 buried under their homes and the women and children killed. The time has come.

outline.heading: The same Muslim everywhere, and ignored
outline.gist: Sit with any Muslim in any masjid and you hear the same hopes, fears and dreams, yet the world makes its decisions with no regard for hundreds of millions of Muslims, and we have accepted being ignored as normal.

outline.heading: Dictatorships and a semi-functional masjid
outline.gist: Well-functioning dictatorships have left little hope, so the bar is a masjid that does not put you to sleep, no daily harassment and enough money for your family.

outline.heading: We raised the financial bar, not the ummah's
outline.gist: Muslims are more comfortable financially than ever, but hopes for the future of the ummah stay embarrassingly low, to the point that people tire of imams raising them.

outline.heading: Why he keeps talking about this
outline.gist: It is all he will talk about, because nothing else is worth it now. Imams in history could discuss abstract topics because their institutions were protected and Muslims were respected; we cannot.

outline.heading: No value in the world: self-censoring at work
outline.gist: We all manoeuvre at work around what we may say, keeping our stances secret even in the masjid, for fear our words will be twisted to paint us as hate-mongers.

outline.heading: A faith that names others as people under its protection
outline.gist: Muslims were never raised to hate any group. Our scripture names people of other faiths as those under our protection: if they live with us, their safety is our responsibility and we ask nothing of them.

outline.heading: Success and failure come from within
outline.gist: Change will come from inside the ummah, from each heart. Allah promised the Prophet He would not destroy his ummah by general punishment nor let an outside enemy uproot it; its harm would come from itself.

outline.heading: A decision only Allah sees
outline.gist: Each of us must make a decision in a place no one but Allah can see, so that Muslims and all people live with dignity, safety and equality, and narratives rest on justice and human rights, the core values Muslims carry.

outline.heading: Dignity for every living thing
outline.gist: Those values extend to every living thing: people have been punished in Hell for mistreating animals, let alone human beings.

outline.heading: Why share maxims: no two people give the same goal
outline.gist: He does not know why minority communities in the West cannot get things done, so he shares his maxims to make agreement and disagreement clear. Whenever he asks what Muslims here are trying to achieve, no two people give him the same answer.

outline.heading: Interlude
Maxim one: permission to teach
outline.gist: To stand on a minbar or talk about the deen you need permission from the scholars who taught you. He gave no khutbah until three teachers granted him partial and then full permission, and preached under their supervision for years; every discipline of knowledge works the same way.

outline.heading: Islam is an oral tradition
outline.gist: The Prophet taught the companions, men and women, face to face, and each generation taught the next; that is why the Quran and his legacy are preserved.

outline.heading: Standing in the Prophet's place
outline.gist: When he came to the city he found Jumuah established with unqualified speakers. He stands in the place where the Prophet should stand, smaller than an atom and ashamed, only because scholars are lacking; opening it to anyone is not safe.

outline.heading: Not from books or YouTube videos
outline.gist: You cannot read a book or watch videos from someone 15,000 miles away and think you are ready to preach the deen.

outline.heading: Bring the scholar first; space is the least problem
outline.gist: We have buildings without scholars. Bring the scholar first and it does not matter whether you teach outside on the lot, on the green or under a tree; youth must spend a decade or two with scholars to be qualified to speak.

outline.heading: The speaker is the one most at risk
outline.gist: He stays up at night going over what he said, because he speaks on behalf of God in the place of Muhammad. Listeners take the best and leave the rest; he will be held accountable for every word.

outline.heading: Prepare scholars of both genders
outline.gist: Unless the deen is transmitted properly, preparing the next generation of imams, scholars and speakers of both genders, it loses its substance. Books document knowledge but are not its source.

outline.heading: Like medical rotations: learning from mentors
outline.gist: No one becomes a doctor from a book; you rotate behind physicians for years, and every physician says the mentor taught them. Islam above all comes through a chain of teachers back to Muhammad.

outline.heading: Room to reflect, within a proper method
outline.gist: None of this removes room for thought, contemplation or reflection; it means respecting a proper educational method.

outline.heading: Interlude
Maxim two: you don't have to agree to work together
outline.gist: Most of your life you will work with people you mostly disagree with. If you walk away at the first obstacle, revisit your intention; obstacles are expected, so find ways to collaborate and show enough respect that everyone can work together.

outline.heading: The believer who mixes with people and bears their harm
outline.gist: In the authentic narration in Ahmad, the believer who works with people and perseveres through their harm is better than the one who isolates himself. Harm is a given, so grow a thick skin.

outline.heading: You are responsible for yourselves: 5:105
outline.gist: O you who believe, you are responsible for yourselves; those who stray cannot harm you if you are guided, and to Allah you all return.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr: 5:105 is no licence to withdraw
outline.gist: Some used the verse to say they owed nothing beyond themselves and could walk away. Abu Bakr told them from the minbar they were misusing it: if people see an oppressor or a wrong in their community and do not stop it, Allah is close to punishing them all.

outline.heading: No clean way out
outline.gist: Accepting Islam makes you part of a group. Only someone who spent his life in dawah and was excluded by all humanity could take a few sheep to a mountain; everyone else must carry the community's pain and hopes until meeting Allah.

outline.heading: No exception for the burnt
outline.gist: People burnt after years in community organizations want nothing more to do with any Muslim institution. However many times you are burnt, you are still part of this community: try again, the sixteenth time may work, or move and work elsewhere, but never in a silo.

outline.heading: Teach your children not to isolate
outline.gist: Teach your teenagers that living on their own is not an option; Muslims who do so are wrong, however good their first intentions.

outline.heading: Sail together or sink together
outline.gist: This is the ummah we have, for better or worse. Change will take sacrifice, collaboration, humility, compassion and hours of hard work; this generation has never had clearer reason to say it is worth it.

outline.heading: Outro

YFMYNmSaQWY.title: Surat Al-Munafiqun, Part 1 (Verses 1-3)
YFMYNmSaQWY.one_line: Al-Munafiqun 1-3: what hypocrisy means, why its signs are for self-examination, oaths used as shields, and judging deeds rather than hearts.
YFMYNmSaQWY.summary: After reviewing how Juz 28 organizes Muslim society, he introduces Al-Munafiqun by defining nifaq from the image of a tunnel: something shown and something hidden. Hypocrisy is an inner condition with signs but no diagnostic checklist, so the Prophet's descriptions are for examining oneself, which is why the companions, Umar pressing Hudhayfah above all, feared it for themselves. Feeling secure in one's own faith is itself a warning sign, since no one can verify a single accepted deed. In verse 1 he shows how the grammar stresses that their testimony was explicit, even made in the Prophet's presence, yet Allah calls them liars: testimony changes nothing about reality and must be proven by one's life. Verse 2 describes oaths used as a shield to enjoy the perks of a functional Muslim community without its heavy demands. He insists Muslims must accept people's outward claims, avoid reducing anyone to a label, and assess actions like an investigator. Verse 3 explains that they believed then rejected the commitment inwardly, so their hearts were sealed and they lose the ability to understand their own lives. He closes by describing Madinah as a mixed community with many numbers but little output, arguing that the ummah's real problem is dead weight, not conspiracies, and that clear action requirements and leadership expose it.

outline.heading: Review: the comprehensive surahs and the Medinan Juz 28
outline.gist: The last four juz summarize the Quran; Juz 28 is late Medinan and organizes relationships within a newly established state.

outline.heading: Al-Mumtahanah recap: categories of non-Muslims
outline.gist: Kafir is a category, not a curse; those at war or oppressing you are not taken as allies, while peaceful non-Muslims receive fairness and kindness.

outline.heading: As-Saff and Al-Jumu'ah recap: social contract and leadership
outline.gist: What the individual owes the group, and leadership the community always has through the minbar.

outline.heading: Nifaq: the tunnel, shown and hidden
outline.gist: The root links spending wealth that disappears and a tunnel; a munafiq shows one thing and hides another, so the group cannot be pointed out.

outline.heading: An inner condition with no diagnostic criteria
outline.gist: Hypocrisy has signs and real effects on the nation, but it is a spiritual matter that cannot be checked off on a list.

outline.heading: The four traits of the hypocrite
outline.gist: Lying in speech, breaking covenants, losing ethics in disputes and betraying trusts, even by someone who prays and fasts.

outline.heading: The signs are for examining yourself
outline.gist: Ask whether you are truthful, trustworthy and ethical in conflict; the companions constantly feared these traits in themselves.

outline.heading: Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his son
outline.gist: The Prophet never publicly named him, yet when he died his believing son asked, and the Prophet prayed over him out of compassion before being told not to.

outline.heading: Ka'b ibn Malik: only the excused or the hypocrite stayed behind
outline.gist: Ka'b saw that those left in Madinah had valid excuses or were known for hypocrisy, a status never formally declared.

outline.heading: Legal categories rest on what is apparent
outline.gist: In this world there are believers and the categories of non-believers by visible status; hypocrite is not a legal category, and each person is judged individually by Allah.

outline.heading: The premise for reading the surah
outline.gist: Descriptions of hypocrites are mirrors for ourselves, not labels for others.

outline.heading: Interlude
Addressed to the Prophet: a surah of incidents
outline.gist: When a surah opens by speaking to the Prophet directly, stories and dynamics follow.

outline.heading: "We bear witness": a testimony made explicit
outline.gist: The grammar implies an omitted question, establishing that their testimony was clear and deliberate.

outline.heading: Allah bears witness that they are liars
outline.gist: Double emphasis frames the exchange, with Allah's knowledge placed in between.

outline.heading: Testimony does not change reality
outline.gist: Whether the world affirms or denies, the Prophet is the Messenger; your testimony is a claim about yourself.

outline.heading: Their testimony was outwardly better than ours
outline.gist: They said it face to face with the Prophet while ours is distant in time and place, yet Allah called them liars.

outline.heading: So how can I say I am not one of them?
outline.gist: If hypocrites cannot be identified and none admits it, the fear should turn inward.

outline.heading: Umar presses Hudhayfah, keeper of the secrets
outline.gist: Hudhayfah knew the hypocrites' names; Umar followed him asking if he was among them until Hudhayfah said no, and Umar wept.

outline.heading: Comfort about one's faith is a warning sign
outline.gist: The great scholars lived in fear; no one can swear a single deed was accepted, so feeling secure reflects a lack of knowledge.

outline.heading: "We shall see": a claim that life must prove
outline.gist: In the hadith qudsi on al-Fatihah, "You alone we worship" is between Allah and His servant; your record must show the belief you claim.

outline.heading: Interlude
Oaths as a shield (junnah)
outline.gist: From the root of hidden and barrier, as in jinn and madness; they used their testimony as protection.

outline.heading: The perks without the buy-in
outline.gist: Islam demands much, while a functional Muslim community offered social security, marriage, support and a voice through shura; they wanted the benefits only.

outline.heading: They turned themselves away from Allah's path
outline.gist: Saddu here refers to turning themselves away, using the shield to do as they wished unquestioned.

outline.heading: Accept the apparent; you cannot know hearts
outline.gist: Muslims must accept people's outward claims; you barely understand your own motives, so do not reduce a person to one word from a gesture.

outline.heading: Judge what they do, like an investigator
outline.gist: The verse condemns what they did; critique actions and evidence, not intentions.

outline.heading: They believed, then disbelieved inwardly
outline.gist: Here iman contrasts with kufr; accepting the testimony but refusing its commitments is kufr before Allah, though outwardly they remain Muslims.

outline.heading: Sealed hearts that no longer understand
outline.gist: Their testimony became a barrier, so Allah placed a barrier over their hearts; they cannot read their own lives, though a changed intention can lift it.

outline.heading: The sinner and the pious man on the hill
outline.gist: Each avoided the other's path; the humble sinner was guided before reaching the top and the self-regarding worshipper deviated before reaching the bottom.

outline.heading: The setting: the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq
outline.gist: The surah's stories took place around the fifth or sixth year after hijrah.

outline.heading: Madinah was not a utopia
outline.gist: It was a mixed community; the Prophet planned on thousands but only a fraction gave or marched, many numbers with little output.

outline.heading: The Quran's diagnosis versus conspiracy talk
outline.gist: Racism, theft and gossip pointed to people who testified without fulfilling the requirements, not to outside plots.

outline.heading: Action requirements and leadership expose dead weight
outline.gist: Hypocrisy is exposed by required commitments of time, wealth and expertise, which needs leadership with a plan; the ummah's problem is dead weight.

Never feel secure about your own faith; keep proving your testimony through your life
Accept people's outward claims and judge actions with evidence, not intentions
Fulfill the commitments of being Muslim with time, wealth and expertise rather than taking only the perks
Read Surat Al-Munafiqun over the week in a standard translation

28:7.ar: وَأَوۡحَيۡنَآ إِلَىٰٓ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰٓ أَنۡ أَرۡضِعِيهِۖ فَإِذَا خِفۡتِ عَلَيۡهِ فَأَلۡقِيهِ فِي ٱلۡيَمِّ وَلَا تَخَافِي وَلَا تَحۡزَنِيٓۖ إِنَّا رَآدُّوهُ إِلَيۡكِ وَجَاعِلُوهُ مِنَ ٱلۡمُرۡسَلِينَ
28:7.en: And We inspired the mother of Moses, saying: Suckle him and, when thou fearest for him, then cast him into the river and fear not nor grieve. Lo! We shall bring him back unto thee and shall make him (one) of Our messengers

28:8.ar: فَٱلۡتَقَطَهُۥٓ ءَالُ فِرۡعَوۡنَ لِيَكُونَ لَهُمۡ عَدُوࣰّ ا وَحَزَنًاۗ إِنَّ فِرۡعَوۡنَ وَهَٰمَٰنَ وَجُنُودَهُمَا كَانُواْ خَٰطِـِٔينَ
28:8.en: And the family of Pharaoh took him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a sorrow, Lo! Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts were ever sinning

28:9.ar: وَقَالَتِ ٱمۡرَأَتُ فِرۡعَوۡنَ قُرَّتُ عَيۡنࣲ لِّي وَلَكَۖ لَا تَقۡتُلُوهُ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَنفَعَنَآ أَوۡ نَتَّخِذَهُۥ وَلَدࣰ ا وَهُمۡ لَا يَشۡعُرُونَ
28:9.en: And the wife of Pharaoh said: (He will be) a consolation for me and for thee. Kill him not. Peradventure he may be of use to us, or we may choose him for a son. And they perceived not

28:10.ar: وَأَصۡبَحَ فُؤَادُ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰ فَٰرِغًاۖ إِن كَادَتۡ لَتُبۡدِي بِهِۦ لَوۡلَآ أَن رَّبَطۡنَا عَلَىٰ قَلۡبِهَا لِتَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ
28:10.en: And the heart of the mother of Moses became void, and she would have betrayed him if We had not fortified her heart, that she might be of the believers

28:11.ar: وَقَالَتۡ لِأُخۡتِهِۦ قُصِّيهِۖ فَبَصُرَتۡ بِهِۦ عَن جُنُبࣲ وَهُمۡ لَا يَشۡعُرُونَ
28:11.en: And she said unto his sister: Trace him. So she observed him from afar, and they perceived not

28:12.ar: ۞وَحَرَّمۡنَا عَلَيۡهِ ٱلۡمَرَاضِعَ مِن قَبۡلُ فَقَالَتۡ هَلۡ أَدُلُّكُمۡ عَلَىٰٓ أَهۡلِ بَيۡتࣲ يَكۡفُلُونَهُۥ لَكُمۡ وَهُمۡ لَهُۥ نَٰصِحُونَ
28:12.en: And We had before forbidden foster-mothers for him, so she said: Shall I show you a household who will rear him for you and take care of him

28:13.ar: فَرَدَدۡنَٰهُ إِلَىٰٓ أُمِّهِۦ كَيۡ تَقَرَّ عَيۡنُهَا وَلَا تَحۡزَنَ وَلِتَعۡلَمَ أَنَّ وَعۡدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقࣱّ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
28:13.en: So We restored him to his mother that she might be comforted and not grieve, and that she might know that the promise of Allah is true. But most of them know not

28:14.ar: وَلَمَّا بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُۥ وَٱسۡتَوَىٰٓ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ حُكۡمࣰ ا وَعِلۡمࣰ اۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نَجۡزِي ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
28:14.en: And when he reached his full strength and was ripe, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good

66:11.ar: وَضَرَبَ ٱللَّهُ مَثَلࣰ ا لِّلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱمۡرَأَتَ فِرۡعَوۡنَ إِذۡ قَالَتۡ رَبِّ ٱبۡنِ لِي عِندَكَ بَيۡتࣰ ا فِي ٱلۡجَنَّةِ وَنَجِّنِي مِن فِرۡعَوۡنَ وَعَمَلِهِۦ وَنَجِّنِي مِنَ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
66:11.en: And Allah citeth an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh when she said: My Lord! Build for me a home with thee in the Garden, and deliver me from Pharaoh and his work, and deliver me from evil-doing folk

12:84.ar: وَتَوَلَّىٰ عَنۡهُمۡ وَقَالَ يَٰٓأَسَفَىٰ عَلَىٰ يُوسُفَ وَٱبۡيَضَّتۡ عَيۡنَاهُ مِنَ ٱلۡحُزۡنِ فَهُوَ كَظِيمࣱ‏
12:84.en: And he turned away from them and said: Alas, my grief for Joseph! And his eyes were whitened with the sorrow that he was suppressing

12:85.ar: قَالُواْ تَٱللَّهِ تَفۡتَؤُاْ تَذۡكُرُ يُوسُفَ حَتَّىٰ تَكُونَ حَرَضًا أَوۡ تَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡهَٰلِكِينَ
12:85.en: They said: By Allah, thou wilt never cease remembering Joseph till thy health is ruined or thou art of those who perish

12:86.ar: قَالَ إِنَّمَآ أَشۡكُواْ بَثِّي وَحُزۡنِيٓ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَأَعۡلَمُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
12:86.en: He said: I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah, and I know from Allah that which ye know not

12:93.ar: ٱذۡهَبُواْ بِقَمِيصِي هَٰذَا فَأَلۡقُوهُ عَلَىٰ وَجۡهِ أَبِي يَأۡتِ بَصِيرࣰ ا وَأۡتُونِي بِأَهۡلِكُمۡ أَجۡمَعِينَ
12:93.en: Go with this shirt of mine and lay it on my father's face, he will become (again) a seer; and come to me with all your folk

12:94.ar: وَلَمَّا فَصَلَتِ ٱلۡعِيرُ قَالَ أَبُوهُمۡ إِنِّي لَأَجِدُ رِيحَ يُوسُفَۖ لَوۡلَآ أَن تُفَنِّدُونِ
12:94.en: When the caravan departed their father had said: Truly I am conscious of the breath of Joseph, though ye call me dotard

18:14.ar: وَرَبَطۡنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ إِذۡ قَامُواْ فَقَالُواْ رَبُّنَا رَبُّ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ لَن نَّدۡعُوَاْ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ إِلَٰهࣰ اۖ لَّقَدۡ قُلۡنَآ إِذࣰ ا شَطَطًا
18:14.en: And We made firm their hearts when they stood forth and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We cry unto no Allah beside Him, for then should we utter an enormity

8:11.ar: إِذۡ يُغَشِّيكُمُ ٱلنُّعَاسَ أَمَنَةࣰ مِّنۡهُ وَيُنَزِّلُ عَلَيۡكُم مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءࣰ لِّيُطَهِّرَكُم بِهِۦ وَيُذۡهِبَ عَنكُمۡ رِجۡزَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِ وَلِيَرۡبِطَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِكُمۡ وَيُثَبِّتَ بِهِ ٱلۡأَقۡدَامَ
8:11.en: When He made the slumber fall upon you as a reassurance from him and sent down water from the sky upon you, that thereby He might purify you, and remove from you the fear of Satan, and make strong your hearts and firm (your) feet thereby

8:5.ar: كَمَآ أَخۡرَجَكَ رَبُّكَ مِنۢ بَيۡتِكَ بِٱلۡحَقِّ وَإِنَّ فَرِيقࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ لَكَٰرِهُونَ
8:5.en: Even as thy Lord caused thee (Muhammad) to go forth from thy home with the Truth, and lo! a party of the believers were averse (to it)

8:6.ar: يُجَٰدِلُونَكَ فِي ٱلۡحَقِّ بَعۡدَ مَا تَبَيَّنَ كَأَنَّمَا يُسَاقُونَ إِلَى ٱلۡمَوۡتِ وَهُمۡ يَنظُرُونَ
8:6.en: Disputing with thee of the Truth after it had been made manifest, as if they were being driven to death visible

8:7.ar: وَإِذۡ يَعِدُكُمُ ٱللَّهُ إِحۡدَى ٱلطَّآئِفَتَيۡنِ أَنَّهَا لَكُمۡ وَتَوَدُّونَ أَنَّ غَيۡرَ ذَاتِ ٱلشَّوۡكَةِ تَكُونُ لَكُمۡ وَيُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ أَن يُحِقَّ ٱلۡحَقَّ بِكَلِمَٰتِهِۦ وَيَقۡطَعَ دَابِرَ ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ
8:7.en: And when Allah promised you one of the two bands (of the enemy) that it should be yours, and ye longed that other than the armed one might be yours. And Allah willed that He should cause the Truth to triumph by His words, and cut the root of the disbelievers

20:96.ar: قَالَ بَصُرۡتُ بِمَا لَمۡ يَبۡصُرُواْ بِهِۦ فَقَبَضۡتُ قَبۡضَةࣰ مِّنۡ أَثَرِ ٱلرَّسُولِ فَنَبَذۡتُهَا وَكَذَٰلِكَ سَوَّلَتۡ لِي نَفۡسِي
20:96.en: He said: I perceived what they perceive not, so I seized a handful from the footsteps of the messenger, and then threw it in. Thus my soul commended to me

8:43.ar: إِذۡ يُرِيكَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ فِي مَنَامِكَ قَلِيلࣰ اۖ وَلَوۡ أَرَىٰكَهُمۡ كَثِيرࣰ ا لَّفَشِلۡتُمۡ وَلَتَنَٰزَعۡتُمۡ فِي ٱلۡأَمۡرِ وَلَٰكِنَّ ٱللَّهَ سَلَّمَۚ إِنَّهُۥ عَلِيمُۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ
8:43.en: When Allah showed them unto thee (O Muhammad) in thy dream as few in number, and if He had shown them to thee as many, ye (Muslims) would have faltered and would have quarrelled over the affair. But Allah saved (you). Lo! He knoweth what is in the breasts (of men)

8:44.ar: وَإِذۡ يُرِيكُمُوهُمۡ إِذِ ٱلۡتَقَيۡتُمۡ فِيٓ أَعۡيُنِكُمۡ قَلِيلࣰ ا وَيُقَلِّلُكُمۡ فِيٓ أَعۡيُنِهِمۡ لِيَقۡضِيَ ٱللَّهُ أَمۡرࣰ ا كَانَ مَفۡعُولࣰ اۗ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ تُرۡجَعُ ٱلۡأُمُورُ
8:44.en: And when He made you (Muslims), when ye met (them), see them with your eyes as few, and lessened you in their eyes, (it was) that Allah might conclude a thing that must be done. Unto Allah all things are brought back

20:39.ar: أَنِ ٱقۡذِفِيهِ فِي ٱلتَّابُوتِ فَٱقۡذِفِيهِ فِي ٱلۡيَمِّ فَلۡيُلۡقِهِ ٱلۡيَمُّ بِٱلسَّاحِلِ يَأۡخُذۡهُ عَدُوࣱّ لِّي وَعَدُوࣱّ لَّهُۥۚ وَأَلۡقَيۡتُ عَلَيۡكَ مَحَبَّةࣰ مِّنِّي وَلِتُصۡنَعَ عَلَىٰ عَيۡنِيٓ
20:39.en: Saying: Throw him into the ark, and throw it into the river, then the river shall throw it on to the bank, and there an enemy to Me and an enemy to him shall take him. And I endued thee with love from Me that thou mightest be trained according to My will

43:41.ar: فَإِمَّا نَذۡهَبَنَّ بِكَ فَإِنَّا مِنۡهُم مُّنتَقِمُونَ
43:41.en: And if We take thee away, We surely shall take vengeance on them

43:42.ar: أَوۡ نُرِيَنَّكَ ٱلَّذِي وَعَدۡنَٰهُمۡ فَإِنَّا عَلَيۡهِم مُّقۡتَدِرُونَ
43:42.en: Or (if) We show thee that wherewith We threaten them; for lo! We have complete command of them

12:22.ar: وَلَمَّا بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُۥٓ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ حُكۡمࣰ ا وَعِلۡمࣰ اۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نَجۡزِي ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
12:22.en: And And when he reached his prime We gave him wisdom and knowledge. Thus We reward the good

19:12.ar: يَٰيَحۡيَىٰ خُذِ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ بِقُوَّةࣲۖ وَءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ ٱلۡحُكۡمَ صَبِيࣰّ ا
19:12.en: (And it was said unto his son): O John! Hold fast the Scripture. And we gave him wisdom when a child

2:269.ar: يُؤۡتِي ٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ مَن يَشَآءُۚ وَمَن يُؤۡتَ ٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ فَقَدۡ أُوتِيَ خَيۡرࣰ ا كَثِيرࣰ اۗ وَمَا يَذَّكَّرُ إِلَّآ أُوْلُواْ ٱلۡأَلۡبَٰبِ
2:269.en: He giveth wisdom unto whom He will, and he unto whom wisdom is given, he truly hath received abundant good. But none remember except men of understanding

DdOBVsNIxys.speaker_note: continues his Friday Arabic tafsir of al-Qasas from last week's verse and recaps the axis he introduced
DdOBVsNIxys.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat al-Qasas, Musa in Pharaoh's House (28:7-14)
DdOBVsNIxys.one_line: Musa's rescue and return to his mother: we are servants not judges, Allah ties the hearts of the steadfast, and tawakkul includes effort.
DdOBVsNIxys.summary: He restates the surah's two lessons: another person's story is too complex for us to judge, yet in itself it runs on simple motives. Formal logic that works in science fails in judging people's ultimate state; we are servants, not judges, and judging is among the most dangerous seats. The scene of Musa's mother casting her baby into the Nile shows how wrong an onlooker would be. Pharaoh, scheming against the decree, ends up raising his own enemy, and he deliberately chose wrong. Asiya's plea makes Musa a coolness of the eye, which he explains as the opposite of eyes hot with weeping. The mother's heart becomes empty of all but her son, and Allah ties her heart so she does not give him away; this tying, as with the youths of the cave and the companions at Badr, means steadfastness, not guaranteed victory. Sending the sister to follow him shows tawakkul is effort plus contentment, and he loses patience with fatalistic talk about why one should work. Allah forbids other nurses so Musa returns to his mother, with Pharaoh paying for it. Allah's promise is true even when the faithful die before seeing it. Musa grows up with sound judgement and knowledge, which every generation of youth needs, and each person should push the ummah's curve upward while life lasts.

outline.heading: Recap: an axis about relationships
outline.gist: Humans live seeking relationships with people, the universe, life, Allah and family; al-Qasas starts with relationships with people through their stories.

outline.heading: Two lessons: complex to you, simple in itself
outline.gist: You lack the knowledge to judge another's story, yet what drives it is simple: pride, envy, showing off, heedlessness, greed.

outline.heading: Formal logic does not judge souls
outline.gist: Syllogisms like 'he is a Muslim, so he is in Paradise' work in science but not in existential and religious judgments about people.

outline.heading: The onlooker at the Nile
outline.gist: A fisherman seeing a mother throw her newborn into the river would condemn her, lacking the facts about Pharaoh's soldiers and Allah's inspiration.

outline.heading: We are servants, not judges
outline.gist: Allah did not place us as judges of people; judging and issuing fatwas bring a person closest to the Fire, so only the most pious should take those seats.

outline.heading: Story after story until it settles
outline.gist: The surah gives example after example of people misjudging; rules for what to do when you see wrong will come later.

outline.heading: Recitation and the length of elongations
outline.gist: In Hafs via ash-Shatibiyyah, elongations are kept at a consistent four counts regardless of how small the mark is written, with few six-count exceptions.

outline.heading: Pharaoh's household picks him up
outline.gist: The river ran through the palace wall; Asiya and the soldiers found the basket, and the verse states the ending first: he would be their enemy and grief.

outline.heading: Khati'in: wrong by choice
outline.gist: The mukhti' errs while seeking the right; the khati' knows and does wrong anyway; Pharaoh scheming against the decree raises his own enemy.

outline.heading: Asiya: her lineage and her rank
outline.gist: Most likely a Copt, not an Israelite; one of the four perfected women, she knew her husband was a tyrant and could not have children.

outline.heading: Coolness of the eye: the opposite of a hot eye
outline.gist: Arabs cursed with 'may Allah heat your eye', meaning endless weeping; a cool eye means lasting happiness.

outline.heading: Pharaoh trapped by his own lie
outline.gist: Having likely told Asiya his soldiers did not kill babies, he could not refuse her; every lie ends in loss.

outline.heading: And they did not perceive
outline.gist: An aside from Allah: no one, not Pharaoh, Asiya or the mother, knew what was being prepared; His decree runs whether they will or not.

outline.heading: An empty heart: the mother's consciousness
outline.gist: The fu'ad is conscious awareness, the qalb holds the subconscious; her awareness emptied of everything but Musa.

outline.heading: A parent's grief: Ya'qub as the closest picture
outline.gist: Only Ya'qub's grief for Yusuf conveys a mother's loss; he prays for every mother who lost a child.

outline.heading: Allah tied her heart
outline.gist: Fear is a powerful driver; she nearly revealed him, but Allah steadied her so she could complete the faith she had begun.

outline.heading: Finish the road you started
outline.gist: All our stories share the same core with different details; once you start on Allah's path, see it through to the end.

outline.heading: Tied hearts: the youths of the cave and Badr
outline.gist: Allah tied the hearts of the cave youths and of the outnumbered companions at Badr who disliked the fight.

outline.heading: Tying the heart means steadfastness, not victory
outline.gist: The youths of the cave did not triumph in life; the promise is that you will not be shaken from your path, whether you win or are killed.

outline.heading: Follow him: qass as tracking traces
outline.gist: Qass is following tracks, the root of qissah; the young sister walked along the bank and caught sight of him from a distance.

outline.heading: Allah controls the details people miss
outline.gist: No one noticed the girl; Allah governs how the mind reads what the eye sees, as at Badr and at the cave during the hijrah.

outline.heading: Tawakkul is effort plus contentment
outline.gist: Sending the sister did not contradict trust; reliance means doing your part while accepting Allah's decree.

outline.heading: Fatalist talk is disrespect to Allah
outline.gist: Asking why work if provision is written is foolish and ill-mannered, especially while the ummah suffers mass killing and normalisation.

outline.heading: Forbidding the wet nurses
outline.gist: Asiya had no milk and the baby refused every nurse; a newborn cannot survive long without feeding, and the sister watched it unfold.

outline.heading: Shall I point you to a household?
outline.gist: Once the news spread she could safely offer a family to nurse and raise him, like the Prophet's nursing among Banu Sa'd.

outline.heading: Returned to his mother, paid by Pharaoh
outline.gist: Instead of raising him in hiding she raised him openly, paid by the very tyrant he would overthrow.

outline.heading: A coolness of the eye for two mothers
outline.gist: Musa was a comfort to Asiya and to his own mother, made under Allah's eye; he kept the name she gave him.

outline.heading: Allah's promise is true: Sumayyah and Yasir
outline.gist: Early martyrs in Makkah died before seeing any promised victory, yet the promise held.

outline.heading: The youths of the cave revived only to see
outline.gist: They were raised after centuries just to see that their stand had turned the kingdom to tawhid, then died; steadfastness, not seeing results, is the task.

outline.heading: Demanding to see results is arrogance
outline.gist: Refusing to work unless promised you will see the outcome is pride; even the Prophet was told he might die before seeing it.

outline.heading: Reaching full strength, raised in two homes
outline.gist: Maturity of body can come before forty; Musa learned the Israelites' knowledge from his mother and lived in the palace knowing who he was.

outline.heading: Tyrants keep the enslaved untrained
outline.gist: A dictator keeps slaves busy with survival; Musa, raised as a prince, was trained in horsemanship and skills.

TGuMlpPLrLg.title: Arabic Tafsir: Opening of Surat al-Qasas (28:1-7)
TGuMlpPLrLg.one_line: Introducing al-Qasas as the surah of human relationships: people are stories we cannot judge, Pharaoh's tyranny, and the promise to the oppressed.
TGuMlpPLrLg.summary: He opens by defending teaching in Arabic as following the Prophet's practice and argues that language carries a culture and spirit, so distance from Arabic leaves a gap with the Quran. He then begins a new axis of five surahs, al-Qasas to as-Sajdah, about relationships, the first being relationships with people. Each person is to us only a story, told from a biased angle, so we cannot judge anyone by what we see or hear; only Allah judges, from the record our deeds write. Yet human stories reduce to simple heart diseases such as pride, envy and fear, which we should use to examine ourselves and help others, not to condemn them. A single moment of sincerity, as when Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik chose Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, can repair great corruption. Explaining the opening verses, he describes Pharaoh's divide-and-rule tyranny, his targeting of the learned Israelites and the slaughter of their sons, and insists a Muslim must never lose mercy even when the enemy has. Real change needs ready people, not only better rulers. The promise to the oppressed comes in stages, and the oppressed must not become oppressors. Every participant in injustice is accountable, with no excuse of following orders. He ends with Musa's mother casting her baby into the Nile, an act any onlooker would misjudge.

outline.heading: Teaching religion in Arabic as a sunnah
outline.gist: Speaking about the deen in the Prophet's language is an act of worship for him; classical eloquence takes years and fades without practice.

outline.heading: Against translation on the minbar
outline.gist: He prefers separate khutbahs in each language; translating mid-khutbah breaks the speaker's train of thought.

outline.heading: Language carries culture and spirit
outline.gist: Children raised here have a different culture and understanding of religion; while you are far from Arabic you remain far from the Quran.

outline.heading: The tafsir journey and the new axis
outline.gist: After covering Ghafir to an-Nas and then al-Ahzab to az-Zumar on obedience and submission, he begins the axis from al-Qasas to as-Sajdah.

outline.heading: An axis about relationships
outline.gist: A relationship is a continuous bond carrying emotion, one of the stages of love in Arabic; these five surahs cover our core relationships, starting with people.

outline.heading: The long-running happiness study and the tribe
outline.gist: A decades-long study found the happiest people had the strongest relationships, not the most wealth or status; tribes were extended families, and Islam came to refine these bonds.

outline.heading: Why al-Qasas: every person is a story
outline.gist: I know you only through the story you tell, which is subjective; your father would tell it differently.

outline.heading: First principle: you cannot judge people by their story
outline.gist: Whether seen, heard from them or about them, stories do not let us judge; only Allah judges, from the record written by deeds, not words.

outline.heading: Second principle: human stories are simple
outline.gist: They reduce to pride, envy, fear, greed; this simplicity is for judging yourself and helping others, never for condemning them.

outline.heading: World calamities come from simple diseases of the heart
outline.gist: Geopolitical misery traces back to arrogance, envy and greed; when a ruler's heart is reformed, much corruption can be undone.

outline.heading: Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik and Abu Hazim
outline.gist: Asked why we love this world and hate the next, Abu Hazim said you built up this world and ruined your Hereafter.

outline.heading: Choosing Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz
outline.gist: In his final illness Sulayman passed the caliphate to Umar rather than his son, and Allah repaired much Umayyad corruption through him.

outline.heading: Review yourself instead of judging others
outline.gist: Check your own deeds for vanity, envy and arrogance; al-Qasas forces you, story after story, to see that you misread what you saw.

outline.heading: A late Makkan surah, partly revealed on the hijrah
outline.gist: Makki and Madani are defined by before and after arrival in Madinah; verses revealed during the hijrah count as Makki.

outline.heading: Ta Sin Mim: recitation rules and the challenge
outline.gist: Lengths of each letter total sixteen counts; the disjointed letters challenge the Arabs, and as-Suyuti grouped surahs sharing them.

outline.heading: After the letters, always the Book
outline.gist: Surahs opening with disjointed letters immediately mention the Quran, underlining the challenge.

outline.heading: The clear Book amid unclear people
outline.gist: Others' motives will never be clear to you, but the Book makes clear what you should do in response.

outline.heading: We recite to you in truth, for people who believe
outline.gist: Tilawah is voicing the written word, unlike deeper reading; the story is full of wonders only a believing heart will accept.

outline.heading: Background first: where Pharaoh ruled
outline.gist: Allah supplies the background we usually lack about people; the setting was the eastern Nile delta, around Goshen.

outline.heading: Pharaoh as a title and the expulsion of the Hyksos
outline.gist: Joseph's Egypt had a king, not a pharaoh; native rulers expelled the Hyksos and punished the Israelites who had sided with them.

outline.heading: Making its people into factions: divide and rule
outline.gist: Pharaoh split Egypt into hostile groups so they would not unite against him; Allah condemns splitting into sects.

outline.heading: The despot targets the learned
outline.gist: Tyrants enslave those with knowledge and morals to corrupt them; boys were slaughtered and girls kept alive for abuse and servitude.

outline.heading: Pharaoh's dream and the slaughter of infants
outline.gist: Told a boy from his slaves would topple him, Pharaoh ordered newborn boys killed, reportedly tens of thousands.

outline.heading: A Muslim never strips mercy from his heart
outline.gist: Cruelty is an old human impulse; if you lose mercy because your enemy did, nothing distinguishes you, and Allah supports the side with morals.

outline.heading: Expecting one oppressor to stop another
outline.gist: Child-killing is not new; what is new is the lack of men to stand against it, and hoping powers that devastated Iraq and Syria will intervene is futile.

outline.heading: Only people of truth end oppression
outline.gist: The meaning of truth, justice and sacrifice faded from the ummah for centuries; rebuilding it takes a generation of awakening.

outline.heading: Change does not come only from the top
outline.gist: Reforming rulers worked in eras when the people were ready; today the problem is also in the people, so reform must start with them.

outline.heading: Recitation: We willed to favour the oppressed
outline.gist: He recites the promise to the oppressed and to Pharaoh's downfall.

outline.heading: The reciter in Jerusalem after the occupation
outline.gist: A famous Egyptian reciter chose this verse in Al-Aqsa; those once oppressed in Egypt now oppress others in the holy land.

outline.heading: The oppressed must not become the oppressor
outline.gist: Without principles, the wronged quickly turn into wrongdoers; Musa did not replace Pharaoh with another ruler but with a prophet.

outline.heading: Leadership of character, not politics
outline.gist: Allah can favour the oppressed in any age; the imamate promised is in morals, knowledge and religion, as with Ibrahim.

outline.heading: The order of the promise
outline.gist: First lifting weakness, then making them leaders, then heirs, then establishing them; once established some reformed and some corrupted.

outline.heading: Haman as a title and what they feared
outline.gist: Haman is likely the office of chief minister; they were shown the very thing they feared, the boy who would end their rule.

outline.heading: Pharaoh, Haman and their soldiers: all accountable
outline.gist: The one who ordered, the one who advised and the soldier who killed a newborn all lacked mercy and will all be judged.

outline.heading: No excuse of following orders
outline.gist: Imam Ahmad told his jailer he was not merely a helper of oppressors but an oppressor; even under threat of death you may not kill an innocent.

outline.heading: Was Musa's mother a prophet?
outline.gist: The stronger view is that prophets were men only and her revelation was inspiration, though some scholars allowed prophethood but not messengership for women.

outline.heading: Hiding the pregnancy and the command to cast him into the river
outline.gist: She hid her pregnancy while serving in palaces and was told to nurse him and, if afraid, cast him into the Nile.

outline.heading: The onlooker would condemn her
outline.gist: A fisherman watching a mother throw her baby into the river would judge her a terrible mother, not knowing the background or Allah's plan.

outline.heading: The oven and the escape to the Nile
outline.gist: She hid him in a cooling oven during a search, then took him to the river; closing dua.

yIZpZRK51UY.title: My Maxims, Part 1: Communal Obligation, the Ummah as the Goal, Following Your Local Imam
yIZpZRK51UY.one_line: Opening a post-Ramadan series: three principles he lives by, on why personal worship exists, what the ummah is, and following local leadership.
yIZpZRK51UY.summary: First of a post-Ramadan series in which the sheikh lays out the self-evident principles that drive his own work, so the community can check whether it shares them. He starts from a question that troubled him through Ramadan: why does the ummah fail to get things done when corrupt politicians and conspiracies afflict everyone else too? His answer is that Muslims are not on the same wavelength about what Islam asks of them. He then gives three maxims. First, personal obligations such as prayer, fasting, zakat and hajj are not ends in themselves; Allah needs nothing from us, so they exist to build the strength, empathy and purity needed to carry a communal obligation, a specific field of service each Muslim keeps up until death. Second, the goal of everything is the ummah, understood as all of humanity to whom the Prophet was sent; individuals and institutions have value only through sincere service, and the moment self-preservation outranks service it is corruption. Third, an ordinary Muslim's job is to follow the local imam who is moving Islamic work forward, or to relocate to a scholar he can follow, rather than undermine local leadership from behind a phone. Standing against everyone who works locally, he warns, only jams the wheels of a community.

outline.heading: Opening
Do not be deceived: Fatir 35:5-7
outline.gist: A passage he calls a statement of our maxims: Allah's promise is true, do not be fooled by this life or by the deceiver, and treat Shaytan as the enemy he is, since he calls his followers to the Fire.

outline.heading: What a maxim is, and why he shares his
outline.gist: A maxim is a self-evident rule you have concluded through life that directs your behaviour and decisions. He wants people to know what drives his work, agree or disagree, because there is no point working together without shared principles.

outline.heading: Why don't we get things done?
outline.gist: At the end of Ramadan he kept asking why the ummah lacks productivity, unity and a voice, and cannot achieve what it wants for itself.

outline.heading: Not conspiracies or corrupt politicians: different wavelengths
outline.gist: Someone is always conspiring and every country has corrupt politicians, yet others still get things done. Perhaps Muslims simply do not agree on fundamentals: we hear what we want, and are not close enough on the same wavelength to hear each other through the static.

outline.heading: What is the Prophet's way?
outline.gist: Whoever turns away from his way is not of him. Reducing that way to externals means we are on different wavelengths; the question is what he would have dedicated himself to in our time and place, which his legacy lets us work out.

outline.heading: Maxim one: personal obligations serve the communal one
outline.gist: Prayer, fasting, zakat and hajj must be done and are the basis of a relationship with Allah, but they are means, not the goal. Allah needs nothing from them; they exist so each Muslim can carry part of the ummah's burden in a specific field.

outline.heading: What each act of worship builds
outline.gist: Allah told the Prophet to pray because he would carry a heavy word; fasting builds strength and empathy for the hungry, hajj returns you to the origin, and zakat purifies wealth so it can be used for good.

outline.heading: Until the day you meet God, easy or hard
outline.gist: Work out what you know how to do and keep doing it until death, for better or worse; this is the door you stand at and the piece the ummah needs.

outline.heading: Which piece of the puzzle is yours?
outline.gist: The ummah is a vast mosaic; your piece may be invisible, but each one added fills part of the gap. Not knowing what your communal obligation is puts us in deep trouble.

outline.heading: The people on the ship
outline.gist: The hadith of the ship: if those above let the lower deck drill a hole for water, everyone drowns; if they stop them, all sail on together.

outline.heading: No retirement plan, and results do not matter
outline.gist: There is no retirement from your communal obligation. You may or may not achieve something great; you meet Allah having seen a need, stood up and done your best. All the Quran's teachings exist to help you do that job better.

outline.heading: After Ramadan, then what?
outline.gist: We filled the masjids and wept as the imam made dua; did we expect a lightning bolt to strike the people we dislike and the earth to turn green? That is not how it works, though some once asked the Prophet simply to make dua and change things.

outline.heading: Dua is the beginning of a different lifestyle
outline.gist: The moment Allah opened your heart in Ramadan was the moment to pledge to serve Him and the people around you until death. If you did not, what did you get out of it?

outline.heading: Maxim two: the Prophet's nation is humanity
outline.gist: A prophet's nation is everyone he was sent to, not only those who believed, and the Quran says he was sent to humanity. Muslims are those who responded; they must protect the message, preserve it and deliver it well.

outline.heading: Only service to the ummah gives value
outline.gist: Individuals, institutions, projects and organizations have no value if their end is not the ummah; there is no room for agendas or self-serving plans.

outline.heading: When self-preservation outranks service, that is corruption
outline.gist: The moment preserving an institution matters more than serving the community, or he says something in his own interest rather than the ummah's, that is corruption.

outline.heading: Start at your doorstep
outline.gist: You cannot serve the whole ummah if you do not serve the people right beside you and help them serve others.

outline.heading: A tired, divided ummah, but ours
outline.gist: It is broken, somewhat defeated and divided, but it is ours, and our only value is what we do for it. Teach this to your children; we owe it to Muhammad to strengthen the ummah so it can carry his message.

outline.heading: The message cannot travel from a weak nation
outline.gist: We were blessed to know the Book and the one who brought it, while many never received it properly. It cannot reach them unless we are a strong nation, which needs strong communities.

outline.heading: Institutions are vehicles; the institution is Islam
outline.gist: This place is only a vehicle to serve the community; the moment it serves itself, tear it down. The real institution is Islam, and every institution within it exists to serve the bigger picture.

outline.heading: Interlude
A school within a school
outline.gist: Teachers who run an after-hours tutoring program inside a school have a clear goal; teachers who open a full rival school inside it are saying the school is wrong and they will overthrow it.

outline.heading: Islam is the group: every institution needs a narrow goal
outline.gist: This place's goal is education and mentorship of young people. An institution that does everything acts as a substitute for Islam, the group-within-a-group phenomenon; we need small groups each focused on advocacy, wealth or mental health. Doing everything is elitism and splits people.

outline.heading: Maxim three: follow your local imam, or move
outline.gist: A common Muslim's job is not to fix every problem but to follow the imam moving Islamic work forward. If you agree with none of the scholars near you, move to one you do; for 1300 years Muslims held that seeking a teacher outranks seeking livelihood.

outline.heading: You cannot follow an imam 15,000 km away
outline.gist: A scholar speaks from his own place and time; follow someone far away while dismissing everyone around you and you cannot be part of your community or further its work.

outline.heading: He never agreed fully with any teacher
outline.gist: He worked with his teachers all his life without agreeing with everything any of them said; you stay together on enough fundamentals.

outline.heading: If everyone local is wrong, go live with the one you accept
outline.gist: He is not telling people to leave, but for your Islamic wellbeing you must live where you can move forward with someone trying to move the Islamic needle.

outline.heading: The pocket sheikh: leadership needs people willing to be led
outline.gist: In masjid after masjid, congregants want the vision of a YouTube sheikh and the imam spends his life asking them to work with him or elsewhere. Islam is wide enough for different paths, but if everyone carries a sheikh in his pocket, the community is horribly hindered.

outline.heading: Abu Hanifa, Hammad and al-Shafi'i
outline.gist: Abu Hanifa listened to many imams for years before settling beside Hammad; when al-Shafi'i left Makkah his students went with him, because a community where you can learn and work is the most valuable thing you have.

outline.heading: Not exclusion: you are obligated to seek it
outline.gist: You deserve to work where the speaker makes sense to you, but you are not entitled to find it where you are; you are obligated to seek it, even by moving, and never to leave it once found.

outline.heading: Why he stayed in Syria on $150 a month
outline.gist: Syria was poor even before the war, and as a resident he earned about 150 dollars a month, but he stayed because his teachers were there; you stay around those who help you grow and serve.

outline.heading: Do not stand against everyone working locally
outline.gist: Being part of a community while calling everyone in it corrupt is unhealthy, un-Islamic and jams the wheels so no one can move forward.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Values, principles and ethics as a system
themes.note: Defines a maxim as a self-evident rule that directs behaviour and argues that a community cannot work together unless it shares a core of principles. The ummah's paralysis, he suggests, comes from Muslims being on different wavelengths rather than from conspiracies or corrupt politicians.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: Following the Prophet's way is not a matter of externals; it means asking what he would have dedicated himself to if he lived here and now, and studying his legacy to answer that.

themes.label: Communal obligation (fard kifayah) as the purpose of personal worship
themes.note: Personal obligations are performed to enable the communal one: prayer builds strength to carry a burden, fasting teaches empathy, hajj returns you to the origin, zakat purifies wealth. Every Muslim must know which piece of the ummah's puzzle is theirs and carry it until death, whatever the results.

themes.label: Dua and invocation
themes.note: The tearful Ramadan dua was not meant to summon a lightning bolt on our enemies; dua is the start of a different way of living, the moment to pledge lifelong service.

themes.label: Community building, cooperation and the ummah
themes.note: The ummah, tired, divided and somewhat defeated, is still ours and is the only measure of value for individuals, projects and institutions. Service begins with the neighbours at your doorstep; a strong ummah needs strong local communities. Teach children that the goal is the ummah.

themes.label: Dawah, outreach and representing Islam
themes.note: A prophet's nation is everyone he was sent to, not only the believers, so the Prophet's ummah is humanity. Muslims are those who responded and now owe it to him to preserve the message and deliver it well to people who have never properly received it.

themes.label: Dawah, outreach and representing Islam
themes.note: The message cannot reach those who never received it properly unless we are a strong nation built on strong communities.

themes.label: Leadership, governance and institutions
themes.note: Institutions are vehicles for serving the community; when preserving the institution matters more than serving people, that is corruption and the vehicle should be dismantled. Islam is the only real institution.

themes.label: Leadership, governance and institutions
themes.note: Sub-groups inside Islam need a narrow, stated goal and must not act as substitutes for Islam (the group-within-a-group phenomenon); doing everything is elitism.

themes.label: Leadership, governance and institutions
themes.note: Leadership only works when people are willing to be led. Congregants who follow a YouTube or pocket sheikh against the local imam's vision are a severe hindrance; he never agreed fully with any of his teachers but kept working with them.

themes.label: Seeking knowledge, learning and scholars
themes.note: Classical practice for 1300 years: you are more obliged to go after a scholar who can teach you than after your livelihood. Abu Hanifa settled on Hammad only after years; al-Shafi'i's students moved with him; he himself stayed in pre-war Syria on a tiny salary because his teachers were there.

3:185.ar: كُلُّ نَفۡسࣲ ذَآئِقَةُ ٱلۡمَوۡتِۗ وَإِنَّمَا تُوَفَّوۡنَ أُجُورَكُمۡ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِۖ فَمَن زُحۡزِحَ عَنِ ٱلنَّارِ وَأُدۡخِلَ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ فَقَدۡ فَازَۗ وَمَا ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَآ إِلَّا مَتَٰعُ ٱلۡغُرُورِ
3:185.en: Every soul will taste of death. And ye will be paid on the Day of Resurrection only that which ye have fairly earned. Whoso is removed from the Fire and is made to enter paradise, he indeed is triumphant. The life of this world is but comfort of illusion

21:35.en: Every soul must taste of death, and We try you with evil and with good, for ordeal. And unto Us ye will be returned

29:57.ar: كُلُّ نَفۡسࣲ ذَآئِقَةُ ٱلۡمَوۡتِۖ ثُمَّ إِلَيۡنَا تُرۡجَعُونَ

21:34.ar: وَمَا جَعَلۡنَا لِبَشَرࣲ مِّن قَبۡلِكَ ٱلۡخُلۡدَۖ أَفَإِيْن مِّتَّ فَهُمُ ٱلۡخَٰلِدُونَ
21:34.en: We appointed immortality for no mortal before thee. What! if thou diest, can they be immortal

4:78.ar: أَيۡنَمَا تَكُونُواْ يُدۡرِككُّمُ ٱلۡمَوۡتُ وَلَوۡ كُنتُمۡ فِي بُرُوجࣲ مُّشَيَّدَةࣲۗ وَإِن تُصِبۡهُمۡ حَسَنَةࣱ يَقُولُواْ هَٰذِهِۦ مِنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِۖ وَإِن تُصِبۡهُمۡ سَيِّئَةࣱ يَقُولُواْ هَٰذِهِۦ مِنۡ عِندِكَۚ قُلۡ كُلࣱّ مِّنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِۖ فَمَالِ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ لَا يَكَادُونَ يَفۡقَهُونَ حَدِيثࣰ ا
4:78.en: Wheresoever ye may be, death will overtake you, even though ye were in lofty towers. Yet if a happy thing befalleth them they say: This is from Allah; and if an evil thing befalleth them they say: This is of thy doing (O Muhammad). Say (unto them): All is from Allah. 9oJFPUCQgBk.title: My Maxims, Part 2
9oJFPUCQgBk.one_line: Prompted by a death close to home, a maxim on mortality: death is the one certainty, so plan for it, stop procrastinating, and fully embrace life.
9oJFPUCQgBk.summary: Continuing his maxims series, he turns to death after a recent loss that hit close to home, noting that months of watching death in the news do not reach us until it is near. In Arabic he gathers the verses that every soul will taste death, that no human was made immortal, that death reaches people even in fortified towers, and that the dying ask in vain to be sent back. He cites the narration that what is most feared for us is following desire and long hope, and Ali's words that the world is departing and the Hereafter approaching, so be its children: today is action without reckoning. In English he recalls being told at 14 that he would die and needed a plan for it. Death is the only certainty and everything else a variable, yet thinking of it should not depress. Procrastination is one of Satan's soldiers, tomorrow is only a hope, and planning for the future is good only when it is for Allah. People feel strangely immune to death, but sayings of Abu al-Darda, Luqman and Imam Ahmad show the early generations lived each day as possibly their last. He closes by saying awareness of death lets us truly enjoy family, love people and work hard, since each of us will one day be forgotten.

outline.heading: Opening
Every soul shall taste death: this week's maxim
outline.gist: He recites 3:185: every soul tastes death, the successful one is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise, and worldly life is only deceptive enjoyment. The maxims are the shared principles we need before working together toward our goals.

outline.heading: Death only registers when it comes close
outline.gist: After learning of a recent death, he notes that months of facing death daily do not sink in until it strikes close to home. The world remains for no one living; only the Ever-Living remains.

outline.heading: No soul is spared: the Quran on death
outline.gist: A chain of verses: every soul tastes death and is tested with good and evil, then returns to Allah; no human before the Prophet was made immortal; death finds you even in lofty towers; the dying beg to be sent back to do good, but behind them is a barrier until resurrection.

outline.heading: Told at fourteen that he would die
outline.gist: Death is coming, so prepare for it and talk about it often. At 14 he was told to his face that he would die and that without a plan for his death he would be miserable and nothing he built would matter.

outline.heading: The one certainty; everything else a variable
outline.gist: Everything in life may or may not happen except one: we die. Thinking about it often is preparation, not a reason for depression.

outline.heading: Sweetness needs the sour
outline.gist: Life holds beauty and ugliness, good and bad; if all you got was ease you would not value it, just as sweetness is enjoyable only because sour and salt exist.

outline.heading: Following desire and long hope
outline.gist: What the Prophet feared most for us was two things: following desire, which turns you from the truth, and long hope, which makes you forget the Hereafter.

outline.heading: Be children of the Hereafter
outline.gist: Ali: the world is departing and the Hereafter approaching, each with its children; be children of the Hereafter, for today is action without reckoning and tomorrow reckoning without action.

outline.heading: Procrastination: tomorrow is only a hope
outline.gist: Procrastination is one of Satan's great soldiers and has deceived many. You do not have time, you have now; none of us is certain of tomorrow.

outline.heading: Three things that make me laugh
outline.gist: The man hoping for the world while death seeks him, the heedless who is not overlooked, and the one laughing aloud not knowing whether his Lord is pleased: he plans years ahead unaware that his next breath may be his last.

outline.heading: Plan the future, for Allah
outline.gist: He is not telling anyone not to plan. Plan for your children and your wealth, but plan for the sake of Allah, so that the future is used for Him.

outline.heading: Three things that make me weep
outline.gist: Parting from the beloved, Muhammad and his companions; the terror of what comes in the throes of death; and standing before the Truth not knowing whether to Paradise or the Fire.

outline.heading: Feeling special at the wrong time
outline.gist: We watch death at every age for months, yet feel a little immune: it will not be me. That is feeling special about the wrong thing. Prepare for what is inevitable; you know people die of heart attacks in their thirties and forties.

outline.heading: Abu al-Darda and Luqman: you are only days
outline.gist: Abu al-Darda: son of Adam, tread the earth, for soon it is your grave; you are only days, and when a day goes part of you goes. Luqman to his son: since you left your mother's womb you turned from this world toward the Hereafter, so you are nearer the home ahead of you.

outline.heading: Interlude
Hostage to 'later' and 'if only'
outline.gist: A poet's line: man is held hostage by 'later' and 'if only', and his ruin lies in them; blessed is the one who managed his affairs and hastened before death.

outline.heading: If anyone were immortal, it would be the Prophet
outline.gist: Death is unavoidable; had anyone been made immortal it would have been the Beloved. Each of us accepts death for others, few for ourselves and those we love.

outline.heading: The death of the young is a reminder
outline.gist: Death comes to the young so that those a few steps from the grave reform themselves; none of us knows in the morning whether he will see the evening, and so lived the righteous.

outline.heading: Imam Ahmad: zuhd is not assuming you will see the evening
outline.gist: Asked what zuhd is, Imam Ahmad said it is that when morning comes your heart does not assume you will reach the evening.

outline.heading: A word you can never unhear
outline.gist: His work is with people being told they will die, a word that once heard can never be unheard. Helping people in their twenties and thirties face their mortality shows how fragile and short life is.

outline.heading: You only live once
outline.gist: Understanding death lets you embrace life for what it is. You only live once, truer than people mean it, so why spend that time on useless things of no value?

outline.heading: How many more Aprils?
outline.gist: We are put here to enjoy the people around us: parents, spouse, siblings, children, friends. A thousand months if you are lucky; how many more Aprils will you see?

outline.heading: Love well, treat people well, work hard
outline.gist: Awareness of death does not take life away; it lets you enjoy it fully. Because time is short you must love well, treat people well, work hard and embrace life rather than watch from the sidelines.

63:4.ar: ۞وَإِذَا رَأَيۡتَهُمۡ تُعۡجِبُكَ أَجۡسَامُهُمۡۖ وَإِن يَقُولُواْ تَسۡمَعۡ لِقَوۡلِهِمۡۖ كَأَنَّهُمۡ خُشُبࣱ مُّسَنَّدَةࣱۖ يَحۡسَبُونَ كُلَّ صَيۡحَةٍ عَلَيۡهِمۡۚ هُمُ ٱلۡعَدُوُّ فَٱحۡذَرۡهُمۡۚ قَٰتَلَهُمُ ٱللَّهُۖ أَنَّىٰ يُؤۡفَكُونَ
63:4.en: And when thou seest them their figures please thee; and if they speak thou givest ear unto their speech. (They are) as though they were blocks of wood in striped cloaks. They deem every shout to be against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them. Allah confound them! How they are perverted

63:5.ar: وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمۡ تَعَالَوۡاْ يَسۡتَغۡفِرۡ لَكُمۡ رَسُولُ ٱللَّهِ لَوَّوۡاْ رُءُوسَهُمۡ وَرَأَيۡتَهُمۡ يَصُدُّونَ وَهُم مُّسۡتَكۡبِرُونَ
63:5.en: And when it is said unto them: Come! The messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you! they avert their faces and thou seest them turning away, disdainful

63:6.ar: سَوَآءٌ عَلَيۡهِمۡ أَسۡتَغۡفَرۡتَ لَهُمۡ أَمۡ لَمۡ تَسۡتَغۡفِرۡ لَهُمۡ لَن يَغۡفِرَ ٱللَّهُ لَهُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ
63:6.en: Whether thou ask forgiveness for them or ask not forgiveness for them is all one for them; Allah will not forgive them. Lo! Allah guideth not the evil-living folk

63:7.ar: هُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ لَا تُنفِقُواْ عَلَىٰ مَنۡ عِندَ رَسُولِ ٱللَّهِ حَتَّىٰ يَنفَضُّواْۗ وَلِلَّهِ خَزَآئِنُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَلَٰكِنَّ ٱلۡمُنَٰفِقِينَ لَا يَفۡقَهُونَ
63:7.en: They it is who say: Spend not on behalf of those (who dwell) with Allah's messenger that they may disperse (and go away from you); when Allah's are the treasures of the heavens and the earth; but the hypocrites comprehend not

IqeWfIBbfTI.title: Surat Al-Munafiqun, Part 2 (Verses 4-7)
IqeWfIBbfTI.one_line: Al-Munafiqun 4-7: hypocrites' polished appearance and inner fear, "they are the enemy, so beware", refusing the Prophet's prayer, and withholding wealth.
IqeWfIBbfTI.summary: He recalls that the Prophet counted his community yet turnout and giving never matched the numbers, which the surah explains as hypocrites who want the perks without the commitment. These verses are for fearing hypocrisy in oneself, since it is a spectrum. Verse 4 portrays people with impressive looks and fine words, like decorative wooden panels with nothing behind them, who live in constant fear of exposure because a lying inner life is unstable. He argues an honest disbeliever is better than a hypocrite, and recalls the Prophet smiling at the Hudaybiyyah clause because those leaving were not needed. "They are the enemy, so beware" is the only time the Quran names a group as the enemy, and the command is caution, not hunting them down: protect the community's work and message from their narratives. Verses 5 and 6 show them turning away in arrogance from the Prophet's offer to seek forgiveness for them, and he explains that persistently walking a path you know is wrong forfeits guidance, the greatest gift. Verse 7 recounts Abdullah ibn Ubayy urging people on an exhausting expedition not to spend on the Prophet's companions so they would desert him. He links charity to truthfulness, notes the Prophet refused to punish Ibn Ubayy, and asks listeners whether they spend their surplus for Allah.

outline.heading: Review: a group neither committed nor declared
outline.gist: Juz 28 organizes Muslim society; the hypocrites are inside the community but do not fulfil the pledge.

outline.heading: The Prophet's census and the missing output
outline.gist: He counted every household, yet far fewer marched, gave or attended than the numbers allowed.

outline.heading: Signs cannot be used to label people
outline.gist: The companions knew not to catalogue people as hypocrites; only Hudhayfah held the names.

outline.heading: Dead weight: benefits without membership
outline.gist: Members receive equal votes, support and defence, so those who give nothing create a damaging imbalance, then and now.

outline.heading: Read the surah to fear for yourself
outline.gist: Testimony benefits only the one who fulfils it; the companions feared hidden hypocrisy in themselves.

outline.heading: Hypocrisy is a spectrum
outline.gist: From habitual untruthfulness to secretly working to destroy Muslims; Allah rejects all of it.

outline.heading: Interlude
Impressive looks and persuasive speech
outline.gist: They keep up appearances and know how to talk; the worst people are the two-faced.

outline.heading: Always ready with an acceptable excuse
outline.gist: After every missed battle they gave reasonable-sounding reasons; the lesson is not to look shabby but that appearance was all they had.

outline.heading: Decorated planks propped against a wall
outline.gist: Like ornamental wooden panels, they look good but have no substance.

outline.heading: Every cry they think is against them
outline.gist: Like a child who broke something, the guilty live in fear of exposure; humans are not built to lie, which is why polygraphs work.

outline.heading: Why an honest disbeliever is better than a hypocrite
outline.gist: The disbeliever is at least clear; the hypocrite received the gift, lied about it and obstructed those who accepted it, so he is in the lowest depth of the Fire.

outline.heading: Hudaybiyyah: why the Prophet smiled
outline.gist: When companions objected that Muslims who left for Makkah would not be returned, he smiled: he did not need those people back.

outline.heading: "They are the enemy"
outline.gist: No faith or nation is called the enemy in the Quran except this group within.

outline.heading: So beware: caution, not a hunt
outline.gist: The command is to be alert so they cannot hijack what you have; Allah will fight and expose them. A masjid's job is to keep their narrative from shaping its teaching and services.

outline.heading: Learn to suit the Quran, not make it suit you
outline.gist: He teaches what Allah says whether liked or not; hypocrites erode morale and slowly bend the texts.

outline.heading: Interlude
"Come, the Messenger will seek forgiveness for you"
outline.gist: Imagine being invited to sit before the Prophet while he prays for your forgiveness.

outline.heading: Love of the Prophet as the opposite of hypocrisy
outline.gist: Later believers would give family and wealth to see him; the companions proved their sincerity by their love of Allah and His Messenger, and love means nothing without commitment.

outline.heading: Turning their heads in arrogance
outline.gist: They refused disrespectfully, so it is the same whether he prays for them or not.

outline.heading: Seventy times and the Prophet's mercy
outline.gist: Seventy signals endlessness; the Prophet said he would ask more than seventy times if it would help, and still prayed for them.

outline.heading: Fasiqun: a path of deviation
outline.gist: Fisq is a way of life one knows is wrong and keeps walking, such as cashing paycheques from a source one knows is unlawful.

outline.heading: Guidance is a gift that can be taken
outline.gist: We ask for guidance at least seventeen times a day; do we value it as much as we claim?

outline.heading: The sinner who thought he was never punished
outline.gist: A voice told him the sweetness of prayer and dua had been taken from him without his noticing.

outline.heading: Interlude
The setting: an exhausting expedition
outline.gist: Likely the Banu al-Mustaliq campaign: worn-out shoes, lost toenails and dwindling provisions; dates of expeditions beyond the milestones are approximate.

outline.heading: "Those with the Messenger": who is in his circle
outline.gist: The hypocrites did not see themselves as those around him; they urged withholding food so the hungry companions would break away.

outline.heading: Abdullah ibn Ubayy's lost crown
outline.gist: He was about to be crowned king of Madinah when the Prophet arrived; he accepted Islam outwardly and withdrew three hundred men at Uhud.

outline.heading: Seventy martyrs and responsibility
outline.gist: Death is by Allah's decree, but those whose actions cause deaths must still be held responsible, as with the killing in Gaza.

outline.heading: Sadaqah as proof of truthfulness
outline.gist: Withholding wealth is a hallmark of hypocrisy; sadaqah comes from sidq and is a clear proof because you put your money where your mouth is.

outline.heading: Why the companions never left him
outline.gist: They had an experience so real nothing could make them leave; holding to rules without that meaning should prompt self-examination.

outline.heading: The treasuries of the heavens and earth
outline.gist: Granting every request of all creation would diminish Allah's dominion no more than a needle dipped in the ocean.

outline.heading: La yafqahun: they lack deep understanding
outline.gist: Fiqh is deep comprehension: knowing your wealth is not yours and can move to others at Allah's will.

outline.heading: He said it openly, and the Prophet refused to punish him
outline.gist: When companions sought permission to execute Ibn Ubayy, the Prophet refused so it would not be said Muhammad kills his companions; ask whether you spend your surplus for Allah.

outline.heading: The quarrel at the well
outline.gist: A scuffle over water at an oasis gave the hypocrites an opening to divide the army.

outline.heading: Outro
